claims.text: The alloy initially contains a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Aging heat treatment causes precipitation of intermetallic compounds.
Precipitation of intermetallic compounds drives the alloy's microstructural evolution.
The intermetallic compounds form through nucleation and growth.
Nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds change the alloy's microstructure.
Nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds change the alloy's composition or compositional distribution.
The type and distribution of precipitated intermetallic compounds determine whether corrosion resistance is retained or lost.
The type and distribution of precipitated intermetallic compounds determine whether high-temperature oxidation resistance is retained or lost.
Temperature and aging time limits exist beyond which the alloy's microstructure and properties are significantly altered.
Aged samples can be compared with unaged samples using microscopy, electrochemical corrosion testing, and thermogravimetric oxidation testing.
The hypothesis is falsified if aging produces no significant difference in either microstructure or corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to unaged samples.
